title: Remembering Eula Phillips
text:
GOOD MORNING!

Remembering Eula Phillips

BY KATHY WILLIAMS
HERALD DEMOCRAT

Nearly 26 years ago I came into the Sherman Democrat newsroom, pretty old for a cub reporter, but the newby nonetheless. Almost the same day, a tough-as-nails older woman walked in. She was wearing a dusty red felt hat, blue jeans and a work shirt of some sort. I never saw her dressed otherwise, except she got a green felt hat once.

She walked right up to me, held out her hand and said, "Who are you? I'm Eula Phillips and I'm your stringer from Savoy." I thought to myself, "I don't care what you call yourself, I'm pretty sure you're Ma Kettle."

Many of you are too young to remember the countrified film figure, who with Pa Kettle ran a ramshackle little farm and cared for a passle of little kids.

Now Eula had money, so her place outside Savoy wasn't ramshackle. She had rent houses. She was nearly 80 before she stopped doing the roof repairs herself. She had dozens of pecan trees and picked and cracked what must have been a ton of them each year.

A stringer, in newspaper parlance, is a person who gets paid by the paper to write specific stories, like covering city council meetings or football games. Eula was a huge advocate for good government, open government, and fiercely confronted secrecy when she suspected the school district or city had something to hide.

She was a great friend over the years. She always greeted me with, "Hey kiddo, how ya doin'?" She had a broad, infectious smile and keen, often dry, wit. She stuck up for herself and for others. She was honest as any landlady ever and helped out those down on their luck, with the requisite grumbling and curmudgeonliness one would expect.

When I read this week that Eula had died, at 90, I was not surprised to learn that she had served as a drill sergeant in the U.S. Army. My heart grew sad for a moment. Then I could hear her say, "Lighten up kiddo and go pick up all those pecans going to waste in that yard of yours."
notes: Column/tribute piece by Kathy Williams. Eula Phillips died at age 90; she was a longtime stringer for the Sherman Democrat covering Savoy, and served as a U.S. Army drill sergeant.
